items.text:
WireGuard site-to-site // Use two peers upstream as central hubs in two different networks to connect the respective peers downstream
&#x200B;

Hello!

&#x200B;

WireGuard is great! And it doesn't take a deep understanding of ip routing to get two clients working. Perfect for me and my little knowledge of ip networking.

My current (test/lab) setup works perfectly when each peer is known to, and connects to, a central peer. This central peer is working like a router forwarding requests to and from each of the peers. Like this:

    A -\   /- D
    B -|-Z-|- E
    C -/   \- F
    

In this setup, Z could have the subnet of [10.10.0.0/16](https://10.10.0.0/16) and each peer just has to forward everything for this subnet for things to work. WireGuard does the magic of routing packages to each peer.

&#x200B;

My goal is something like a site-to-site connect like this:

    Site One   |   Site Two
      A -\           /- F
      B -|-D ----- E-|- G
      C -/           \- H
    subnet 10     subnet 20

Every peer in Site One would connect to peer 'D' and forward everything to subnet [10.0.0.0/](https://10.10.0.0/16)8 to 'D'.

Every peer in Site Two would connect to peer 'E' and forward everything to subnet [10.0.0.0/](https://10.10.0.0/16)8 to 'E..

Peer 'D' would forward everything for subnet [10.20.0.0/16](https://10.20.0.0/16) to peer 'E'. And peer 'E' would forward everything for subnet [10.10.0.0/16](https://10.10.0.0/16) to peer 'D'.

That way, Peers 'D' and 'E' would route packages between each other for all respective peers downstream of themselves (or "behind" them from a central point of view). 

&#x200B;

I have tried a zillion things, sometimes silly and just for sakes' sake, but can not get it to work. Although this is fun, I also ran in a lot of problem with Windows clients, AWS EC2 instances without firewalls, Azure VMs with restrictive security groups, etc. Whenever I fixed one thing, something else popped up. (me: [https://youtu.be/AbSehcT19u0](https://youtu.be/AbSehcT19u0)) 

At some point, I was feeling that maybe my desired scenario is simply out of scope of WireGuard. It certainly is out of scope of my knowledge, but I am ready to learn. I just need to know:

Is a site-to-site connect like described above technically possible \[with WireGuard\] ?

&#x200B;

If so, I'll dive in again.

Yes, subnets are different in each network (ex peers A to D use 10.10.x.y and peers E to H use 10.20.x.y). 

The subnets are just examples. It gets more difficult with AWS LightSail requiring a 172.16/16 Azure wanting 10/8, my home lab using 192.168/16 etc.  

But thats just numbers. I still need to wrap my head around the logic behind the AllowedIPs subnet handling. 

Your post confirms that it can work. Now I just need to work out how. I‘ll get there. Eventually. 🙃
Thanks again.

Settings are saved in the .DS_Store file in each folder.  Delete them if you have problems with settings not sticking.
It doesn‘t look as if it is swapping at all. Why would you assume it is swapping/that the main RAM is full?

What I mean is that once a folder window is arranged in a certain way (say the font size is adjusted) then this is saved to the .DS_Store file of this folder. After that the setting is recalled from the file every time the folder is opened. 

Rearranging other folder does not change anything for the folder with a .DS_Store setting. 

That allows for certain folders to have a different setting (if so configured) than the global one, which is defined as described by you.

Unix always initializes swap. Has nothing to do with use. And 400 MB compared to 16 GB is nothing. 

Its not swapping.

„lol“

More detail:

What you see in column "Memory" is not what you think it is. The RAM a process really uses is shown in the aptly named column "Real Mem", which you might want to show (View > Columns >...).

While you are at it, also show column "Purgable Mem" which shows how much RAM each process would give up - if it has to, but will do, before active processes are swapped.

The amount of "Swap Used" which you identified as a problem is none. That is stuff the system stored there to make space as you approach your 16 GB limit. And it will most likely stay there until you reboot, even if you closed down everything else. 

It would be a problem, if that amount is something like ¼ of your RAM, say 4GB. 

To identify that quickly you have the "Memory Pressure" graph. It graphically represents how efficiently your memory is serving your processing needs. Memory pressure is determined by the amount of free memory, swap rate, wired memory and file cached memory. As long as it is green, everything is fine.

For more info on why the display of the "Activity Monitor.app" Memory column is so weird (and it is), that is basically only "top" being displayed. Unix memory management is != Windows.
See here: https://serverfault.com/questions/48582/how-is-memory-usage-reported-in-linux/48610#48610
and here: https://serverfault.com/questions/138427/what-does-virtual-memory-size-in-top-mean

WPAD stands for "Web Proxy AutoDiscovery". It's your Windows machine trying to find out (by a direct call) if there is a proxy in the way it needs to take into account. Absolutely benign, but annoying.

You can turn this off by adding a line to c:\\Windows\\System32\\drivers\\etc\\hosts that looks like this

    127.0.0.1  wpad.local
